transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-13
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Nebula ML Eng), Tom Alvarez (Nebula Infra), Janelle Park (Nebula VP Product)

Summary:
Quick Optimize module walkthrough focused on INT8 vs FP8 quantization profiles, quality vs latency tradeoffs. Customer wants to understand expected latency improvements, potential quality regressions, and what benchmarking Redwood will run for their LLM workloads (mix of chat & summarization). Security and deployment constraints briefly discussed (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Next steps agreed: share benchmarks, sample prompt set, and schedule poc scoping.

Topics:
- Quantization basics (INT8 vs FP8)
- Redwood Optimize: profile generation and recommendations
- Quality vs latency graphs and thresholds
- Benchmark plan for Nebula sample workload
- Security considerations for Private/Dedicated deployment

Transcript:
[00:00] Laura: ok, hi everyone thanks for joining, um I'm Laura from Redwood, AE on the account, this is Marco who will run through the Optimize quantization walkthrough.
[00:08] Priya: hi Laura, hi Marco, thanks, excited — we are trying to understand the real world tradeoffs. we've got latency targets for our chat product and want to see where INT8 vs FP8 lands.
[00:18] Marco: awesome, quick agenda — we'll cover what each quant profile does, how we measure quality regressions, show some baseline numbers, and then propose a benchmark we'll run on your data.
[00:28] Janelle: quick question — we care about both cost and latency, but product cares more about user-perceived quality. if there's a small regression in summarization, that could be bad.
[00:36] Marco: totally get it. so high level, INT8 tends to give the biggest cost/latency wins but can introduce bit more visible degradation on certain model ops; FP8 is kind of a middle ground — smaller latency improvement than INT8, but often preserves more of the original float32 quality.
[00:50] Tom: and this is across hardware? like A100 vs H100, doesn't the speedup vary a lot?
[00:56] Marco: yes, exactly. H100 has native support and FP8 kernels are much faster on H100, so FP8 can be extremely attractive there. on older hardware INT8 with optimized kernels can still win. we'll show per-hardware curves in a sec.
[01:12] Priya: can you explain what you mean by "profile"? is that per-layer quantization?
[01:17] Marco: good question. profile = the per-layer/operation quantization configuration we generate using Redwood Optimize. it's not just a single global scale — we do per-matrix profiling, some layer-wise mixed precision configs, and we recommend quant ops per block based on sensitivity analysis.
[01:30] Laura: and we store those profiles in the model artifact so you can pin them for rollouts.
[01:35] Janelle: so you'd produce, like, an INT8 profile and an FP8 profile for the same model and we can A/B them?
[01:40] Marco: exactly, and the platform supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback if quality droops below threshold.
[01:46] [01:46] Marco: OK showing slide — here is a sample quality vs latency plot (note: numbers are approximate).
[02:00] Marco: baseline float32 latency on H100: 42 ms p90 per-token for our 7B style model with a 1k context. INT8 reduces to ~28–30 ms p90, FP8 to ~34–36 ms p90. quality-wise, on summarization tasks, BLEU/ROUGE-style metrics drop ~2–4% for FP8 and ~4–8% for INT8 depending on prompt types.
[02:28] Priya: 4–8% drop sounds worrying. How does that map to human eval/subjective quality — do you have examples?
[02:34] Marco: yep, so we do both automated and human evals. automated metrics can overstate regressions. our human eval on a 200-sample set often shows FP8 is indistinguishable from float32 in many cases; INT8 is more noticeable on long-range summarization and certain generation patterns (lots of factual recall).
[02:53] Tom: what's the calibration step? do you need a calibration dataset? how big?
[02:58] Marco: for INT8 we typically run a calibration pass using 1–5k sentences, depending on model size and diversity. for FP8 calibration is cheaper and often optional for some kernels, but we still run sensitivity profiling on a few hundred samples.
[03:12] Priya: ok, our typical prompt mix is about 70% short chat turns and 30% longer summarizations — would you expect INT8 to be worse for that mix?
[03:20] Marco: yes, with more long summarization content you'd see larger quality delta with INT8. FP8 might be the right compromise there. Also you can do hybrid profiles: keep certain sensitive layers in FP16/FP32 and quantize others to INT8 to get most benefits with minimal quality loss.
[03:36] Janelle: hybrid sounds promising. are hybrid profiles automated?
[03:40] Marco: yes we generate them automatically by sensitivity scoring; the Optimize tool outputs a ranked list of layers and recommended precision. you can also hand-edit if you want to be conservative in early rollouts.
[03:49] [03:49] Laura: for cost modeling — we show per-token cost since that's how you bill. INT8 typically reduces GPU memory footprint and increases throughput, so you can reduce instance count or move to cheaper instance families. FP8 gives smaller but still meaningful cost improvements.
[04:10] Priya: how about KV cache compatibility? we use long conversations with caching; does quantization affect KV cache correctness/perf?
[04:16] Marco: good callout — quantization doesn't change KV cache semantics; however, the runtime path can change and that affects memory layout and cache throughput. we test end-to-end with KV cache enabled in our benchmarks. sometimes INT8 paths have more aggressive packing which affects chunking, but nothing that affects correctness.
[04:33] Tom: security question — if we go Private with Redwood, can we still use Optimize and have the profiling happen in our VPC?
[04:40] Laura: yes, Private supports running Optimize entirely inside your VPC. we can run profile generation in your environment; our control plane will orchestrate but the data never leaves your network when configured for on-prem/Private.
[04:53] Priya: and key management? we need KMS/HSM integration for model keys and logs.
[04:58] Laura: we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and support HSM-backed keys for critical artifacts; we'll include the security pack with the integration notes.
[05:07] Priya: excellent.
[05:09] Marco: ok moving on to a sample benchmark plan for Nebula. step 1: we take your prompt set (you provide), step 2: we run float32 baseline on both A100 & H100, step 3: run FP8/INT8 profiles and hybrid configs, step 4: run automated metrics + small human eval on the most-sensitive buckets (summarization, retrieval-augmented responses).
[05:31] Marco: expected deliverables: quality vs latency CSVs, cost-per-token estimates, recommended profile and rollout plan, and a short recording summarizing key findings.
[05:43] Janelle: who owns the risk if we hit a regression in production? like if we roll out INT8 and see a drop in NPS — what's the rollback story?
[05:52] Marco: Redwood supports automatic fallback policies by route — you can set thresholds on quality signals (from automated tests or your production signals) and traffic gets shifted to float32 or FP16 variants. we also support canary windows and manual rollback. for mission-critical flows we usually recommend a hybrid or FP8 first.
[06:09] Priya: can you show an example of a per-layer sensitivity report?
[06:13] Marco: yep, sharing screen now — apologies if the slide labels are fuzzy, the PDF OCR sometimes gets weird — but here's a sample table: Layer 0..3 sensitivity low, Layers 4..7 medium, attention heads more sensitive, feedforward matrices tolerate INT8 better.
[06:33] Priya: ok that maps with our internal experiments. we saw attention heads are the problem.
[06:38] Marco: exactly — thus we often keep attention-proj in FP16 and quantize the MLPs.
[06:43] [06:43] Priya: any runtime gotchas around batching? our workload is bursty.
[06:47] Marco: Redwood's serving runtime supports continuous batching and dynamic batching policies; quantized kernels interact with batching — sometimes larger batches amplify quantization artifacts slightly because of different accumulation behavior, so we include batch-size sensitivity in the profile.
[07:04] Tom: do you support mixed instance fleets? like route some traffic to Dedicated capacity and overflow to Hosted?
[07:09] Laura: yes, smart routing is supported — policy-based routing by latency, cost, or region. you can keep a small Dedicated pool and burst to Hosted.
[07:18] Janelle: how deterministic are the latency numbers? we need p90 and p99 targets.
[07:23] Marco: p90 is usually stable across runs; p99 depends on tail events — we instrument with tracing and can provide per-route p90/p95/p99. quantization generally improves p90 because throughput is higher; p99 improvements depend on infra.
[07:36] [07:36] Marco: ok switching to a real example we ran for "Zenith" — their summarization workload with similar prompt mix: float32 p90 60ms, FP8 44ms, INT8 32ms. human eval on hallucination / factuality changed from 91% correct to 90% for FP8 and 86% for INT8 on a 500-sample set.
[07:58] Priya: so FP8 is basically neutral, INT8 more risky.
[08:02] Marco: that's the pattern we see often. but on H100 FP8 sometimes matches float32 very closely because of the kernel fidelity.
[08:11] Tom: you mentioned model compilation / kernel selection earlier — how automated is that?
[08:16] Marco: it's automated in the runtime. we have a compilation step that selects kernels per op based on model archetype, sequence length, and hardware. Optimize emits a recommended kernel map along with the profile.
[08:29] Priya: do we need to retrain or any fine-tuning for quantization?
[08:32] Marco: typically no. We avoid quant-aware training in most cases by relying on calibration and per-layer scaling. for extreme low-bit quant (below INT8) you might need QAT, but INT8/FP8 usually don't require retraining.
[08:46] Janelle: procurement/security question — if we sign up for Dedicated, what's the SLA and do you provide audit logs for each inference request?
[08:54] Laura: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed throughput and uptime, and we provide request-level audit logs for the last X days depending on retention tier; we can increase retention for enterprise packages.
[09:06] Priya: and what about data retention for prompts/outputs used for optimization? we don't want PII stored.
[09:12] Laura: we support redaction and can run profiling on ephemeral data in your VPC; we can also configure Optimize to only accept synthetic or redacted samples. details will be in the security pack.
[09:23] Tom: ok, real world numbers for cost — can you ballpark cost reduction in $$ per 1M tokens moving to INT8?
[09:30] Marco: rough ballpark: depends on instance pricing, but on average customers see 20–45% unit cost reduction moving to INT8 vs float32, FP8 around 10–25%. we'll produce specific cost-per-token numbers in the benchmark deliverable for Nebula.
[09:48] [09:48] Marco: demo time — I'm going to show the Optimize UI in Redwood Console. apologies for any OCR type mislabels, the demo transcript sometimes picks up weird words.
[09:57] Marco: here is the Profiles tab — you can upload sample prompts or point to a dataset in S3 (or run in-VPC path). we auto-run sensitivity and then propose profiles: INT8-default, FP8-default, hybrid-safe.
[10:12] Marco: clicking into the profile you can see per-layer recommendation, estimated latency improvement, and an estimated quality delta score (0–100).
[10:22] Priya: what's that quality delta score based on?
[10:25] Marco: it's a weighted combination of automated metric regressions (ROUGE, exact match), embedding-based similarity, and a small language-model-based flavor-score we use internally. it's meant as a rough ranking, not an absolute.
[10:38] Janelle: is there an approval workflow to push profiles into production?
[10:42] Marco: yes — profiles can be promoted with canary %s and approvals; you can require an SRE or product owner approval step.
[10:48] Tom: how do you measure user-visible regressions? we have telemetry that looks at completion length and re-rates.
[10:55] Marco: you can plug your production signals into Redwood's alerting; we also support synthetic monitors that run your critical prompts continuously and alert on quality drift.
[11:06] Priya: for human eval you mentioned a small sample — do you run that or do you ask us to run it?
[11:11] Marco: we can run a small blinded human eval for you as part of the benchmark deliverable; if you prefer to run it internally we provide the tools and templates.
[11:20] [11:20] Laura: quick interjection — pricing note: human eval add-on is a billed service, we'll include it in the proposal.
[11:28] Priya: fine. do you have an example CSV of the deliverable?
[11:31] Marco: yes sending a sample — it has columns: prompt_id, prompt_type, baseline_score, fp8_score, int8_score, human_delta, latency_baseline_ms, latency_fp8_ms, latency_int8_ms, recommended_profile.
[11:47] Janelle: how long does the benchmark typically take?
[11:50] Marco: for a 5k-sample benchmark across two hardware types ~48–72 hours including human eval setup. if we parallelize it in your infra it can be faster.
[12:00] Priya: what about conversational state & retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)? we call out to a vector DB — any issues?
[12:06] Marco: no functional issues; we test full RAG loop. the main area to watch is latency added by retrieval; quantization affects only model inference. we look at end-to-end p90/p99 in our deliverable.
[12:18] Tom: do you have any public benchmarks or papers?
[12:21] Marco: we have internal benchmark reports and a few whitepapers; we'll link the relevant ones in the follow-up.
[12:27] [12:27] Marco: ok switching back to the console — here's the canary rollout UI where you choose profile, % traffic, and can attach monitors.
[12:38] Priya: curious about automatic fallback — what signals can trigger it?
[12:42] Marco: you can use synthetic monitor failures, dropped accuracy on known prompts, or custom prod signals (e.g., increase in user corrections) — we hook into your telemetry via webhooks.
[12:54] Janelle: do you store the profiles with model versions? we might have multiple model variants.
[12:59] Marco: yes each model artifact stores associated profiles and the runtime will pick the correct kernel map for the selected profile and hardware.
[13:08] Priya: any caveats about quantizing instruction-tuned models vs base models?
[13:12] Marco: instruction-tuned models sometimes have more sensitive heads post fine-tuning; we recommend profiling the tuned variant rather than assuming base model results. often tuned models show slightly more sensitivity in generation style.
[13:24] [13:24] Tom: infrastructure question — if we run profiling in our VPC do you need any extra roles or agents?
[13:29] Laura: we provide a small agent or a containerized job you can run in your cluster; it uploads only metrics unless you opt into log shipping. we'll provide a secure onboarding doc.
[13:40] Priya: that sounds ok.
[13:42] Marco: quick demo — here's a sample sensitivity heatmap, attention layers highlighted; you can toggle to see hybrid profile suggestions.
[13:51] Priya: thank you, that visual helps.
[13:54] Laura: are there any blockers from our side to start the benchmark?
[13:58] Priya: we'll need to get legal to sign a data processing NDA, and Tom needs clarification on network access for the profiler.
[14:06] Tom: yes, we don't want any outbound access except to your control plane endpoint when allowed.
[14:11] Laura: understood — we'll send our security pack and a diagram of the agent network requirements.
[14:18] Marco: ok, final example — here's a quality vs latency frontier where each dot is a profile: you can pick a point that meets your latency SLO while minimizing human eval delta.
[14:28] Janelle: for our 200ms p90 SLO we need per-token p90 below X, do you have an example mapping?
[14:34] Marco: yes we'll map end-to-end; the per-token numbers we showed will translate into end-to-end p90 for your prompt length in the benchmark deliverable.
[14:44] [14:44] Priya: small nit — when you say p90 per-token is 42ms, is that p90 for a single token or p90 for overall completion latency?
[14:50] Marco: it's per-token p90 for generation. end-to-end completion p90 depends on sequence length, so we'll compute both.
[14:57] Priya: got it.
[15:00] Marco: ok jumping to FAQ slide — Q: Will quantization affect determinism? A: quantization can change determinism slightly because of different numeric behavior; if you need perfect bit-by-bit reproduction we recommend keeping critical flows unquantized.
[15:16] Janelle: good to know.
[15:19] Tom: what about library/tooling support — do you need specific versions of CUDA or Triton?
[15:24] Marco: yes we require certain runtimes; our onboarding doc will list supported CUDA/Triton and driver minimums per hardware.
[15:33] Priya: is there a way to preview the delta for a single prompt in the console?
[15:38] Marco: yes, there's a "compare" mode where you run a prompt across profiles and see side-by-side outputs and metric diffs. it's useful for edge case checks.
[15:48] Priya: we have some prompts with code generation; is quantization safe there?
[15:53] Marco: code generation can be sensitive — we usually recommend FP8 or hybrid for code-heavy flows. we'll make sure to include code prompts in the benchmark.
[16:03] [16:03] Laura: ok, wrapping up — quick recap of agreed items and owners.
[16:08] Laura: Marco will run the FP8/INT8 benchmarks on Nebula's sample set, Priya will share prompts, Tom will unblock network and security requirements, Laura will send security & pricing.
[16:20] Priya: timeline works for us. one ask — can you include a short doc on "how to interpret the quality delta" for our PMs?
[16:27] Laura: yes we'll include a plain-language guidance doc.
[16:30] Marco: I'll add notes about hybrid profiles and recommended canary percentages for different risk tolerances.
[16:37] Tom: one more infra Q — do you provide Terraform or IaC for Dedicated deployment?
[16:42] Laura: yes we have Terraform modules and deployment templates; we'll share a starter repo.
[16:47] Janelle: thanks this was helpful.
[16:49] Priya: thanks everyone.
[16:50] Laura: thanks all, we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and security pack.
[16:55] [16:55] End of meeting.
